accreditation.title: Accreditation, AHEP and the IET
accreditation.content:
The short version

AHEP is the Engineering Council’s standard for what an engineering degree has to teach. It’s a list of 18 learning outcomes.
The IET (Institution of Engineering and Technology) is licensed by the Engineering Council to check degrees against AHEP and accredit them.
An accredited BEng (Hons) partly meets the education requirement for Chartered Engineer (CEng). You’d still need further learning and work experience later.
Every module on this course is written against AHEP. Each module learning outcome is tagged with the AHEP outcome it covers, e.g. [AHEP:4-C9]. Year 1 already touches 17 of the 18.
The course is new, so it isn’t accredited yet. WMG plans to seek accreditation, but it can’t be guaranteed until it’s granted. Our cohort’s work is part of the evidence.



                  
                  Not official 
                  
                

This is my own summary from the module documents, the Warwick course page and the IET and Engineering Council guidance (October 2026). Check the course handbook or ask WMG for the official position.


How the pieces fit together
Engineering Council
 ├── UK-SPEC ── what a registered ENGINEER must show  (competence areas A–E)
 └── AHEP ───── what an accredited DEGREE must teach   (learning outcomes 1–18)
        │
        ▼
 IET (licensed institution)
 ├── accredits degree programmes against AHEP
 └── registers people against UK-SPEC (EngTech · IEng · CEng)

AHEP and UK-SPEC are two halves of the same system. AHEP covers the education part of becoming registered. UK-SPEC covers the competence you show afterwards at work. See UK-SPEC and professional registration for the five competence areas.
The AHEP learning outcomes
AHEP 4th edition (2020) has 18 outcomes, in five groups. Each has three versions:

C1–C18: Bachelors (Hons), partly meeting CEng. This is the set our course uses.
M1–M18: integrated MEng, fully meeting CEng.
B1–B18: Bachelors, fully meeting IEng.

The C and M versions talk about complex problems, and the B versions about broadly-defined ones.




































































































GroupNo.Outcome (paraphrased)Science and mathematics1Apply maths, statistics, science and engineering principles to solve complex problemsEngineering analysis2Analyse complex problems from first principles to reach supported conclusions3Select and use computational and analytical techniques to model problems, knowing their limits4Find and critically evaluate technical literature and other informationDesign and innovation5Design solutions that meet user, societal and business needs within standards and constraints6Use an integrated or systems approachThe engineer and society7Evaluate environmental and societal impact and minimise harm (sustainability)8Identify ethical concerns and make reasoned choices using codes of conduct9Use a risk management process to identify, evaluate and reduce risk10Take a proportionate approach to security risks11Take an inclusive approach: equality, diversity and inclusionEngineering practice12Use lab and workshop skills to investigate problems13Select and apply materials, equipment, technologies and processes, knowing their limits14Understand quality management and continuous improvement15Apply engineering and project management, commercial context and legal matters (including IP)16Work effectively as an individual, a team member and a leader17Communicate complex engineering to technical and non-technical audiences18Plan and record your own learning and development (CPD)
How Year 1 maps to AHEP
These tags come from each module’s own learning outcomes, as listed in the module descriptions and assessment briefs.





































ModuleLearning outcomes and their AHEP tagsWM1AD Electrical Power and MotorsDescribe motor types (C2) · calculate circuit parameters (C1) · justify motor selection (C3) · test motors (C12)WM1AC Mechanisms and MachinesClassify mechanisms (C2) · kinematics (C1, C3) · kinetics (C1, C3) · select actuators (C12)WM199 Developing an Engineering MindsetReflect and set development goals (C18) · identify harm and plan risk reduction (C9) · system requirements (C6) · engage stakeholders (C11) · evaluate sources (C4)WM1AA Rapid PrototypingStatic loading problems (C5) · sustainable design and CAD (C7, C13) · prototypes that pass QC (C12, C14)WM1AE Programmable ElectronicsMicrocontroller applications (C2) · logic for control (C1) · implement, test and debug code (C3, C12)WM1AF Engineering Systems DesignLifecycle models and MBSE (C6) · system models (C3) · systems engineering analyses (C9, C10) · design specifications (C5)WM1AB Mechatronics Sprint ProjectRisk assessment (C9, C15) · concept design (C5, C17) · team detailed design (C6, C7, C17) · safe manufacture (C12, C13) · reflect and present (C11, C16, C17)
The same thing, by outcome

















































































AHEPWhere it shows up in Year 1C1 Science and mathsWM1AD · WM1AC · WM1AEC2 Problem analysisWM1AD · WM1AC · WM1AEC3 Analytical toolsWM1AD · WM1AC · WM1AE · WM1AFC4 Technical literatureWM199C5 DesignWM1AA · WM1AF · WM1ABC6 Systems approachWM199 · WM1AF · WM1ABC7 SustainabilityWM1AA · WM1ABC8 EthicsNot a tagged outcome in Year 1, though WM199 teaches it (Engineering ethics and duty of care)C9 RiskWM199 · WM1AF · WM1ABC10 SecurityWM1AFC11 InclusionWM199 · WM1ABC12 Practical skillsWM1AD · WM1AC · WM1AE · WM1AA · WM1ABC13 Materials and technologyWM1AA · WM1ABC14 QualityWM1AAC15 Management and commercialWM1ABC16 TeamworkWM1ABC17 CommunicationWM1ABC18 CPDWM199
Year 1 introduces almost every outcome at a basic level. Years 2 and 3, especially the final-year project, are where they have to be shown at the full “complex problem” standard.
How accreditation will happen for this course

Status: Warwick says WMG aims to seek accreditation that partly meets the CEng education requirement, and that it can’t be guaranteed at this stage. WMG’s established degrees are already accredited.
When: the IET won’t accredit a new BEng until its final year is running, and normally looks at graduate outputs, mainly final-year project reports. For us, that means around 2028–29.
Backdating: when a programme is accredited for the first time after producing graduates, the IET can backdate accreditation to cover earlier intakes, as long as there’s evidence of those cohorts’ outputs. That’s how first cohorts are normally covered.
Since 2022–23, accreditation for IEng as well as partial CEng isn’t automatic. The IET has to see both sets of outcomes mapped separately.
Keep an eye on: the handbook rules on progression. Some modules carry conditions on staying on the accredited version of the course.

What this means for you

Keep your work. Save every submitted assessment, its feedback, and your lab data. As the first cohort, our work is the evidence for accreditation, and it’s your own record too.
Read the AHEP tags on each brief. They tell you what the assessment is really testing. A brief tagged C9 wants a proper risk process, not just a list of hazards.
Start a CPD log now (CPD log template). It covers C18 and is exactly what the IET asks for when you apply for registration later.
Consider IET student membership. It’s cheap for the whole course, and it gives you events, a mentor network and an earlier start on the route to registration.

The route to Chartered Engineer
Accredited BEng (Hons)  ──►  Further learning  ──►  Experience at work  ──►  Professional review  ──►  CEng
  (partial CEng, AHEP C)      (accredited MSc, or      (show UK-SPEC A–E,      (application + interview
                               learning at work)         usually 4–7 years)      with two CEngs)

An accredited BEng on its own leads more directly to IEng, if the degree is accredited for it. CEng needs Master’s-level learning on top: an accredited MSc, an MEng if WMG adds one, or further learning assessed at work.
Sources

Engineering Council, AHEP 4th edition learning outcomes table
IET, Academic accreditation information pack 2026–27
University of Warwick, BEng Robotics Engineering with Artificial Intelligence
Module learning outcomes: WMG module descriptions and assessment briefs, 2026–27

careers-and-development/applications-and.title: Applications and interviews
careers-and-development/applications-and.content:
The usual stages

Online application: CV, sometimes a cover letter or short questions (“Why this company?”)
Online tests: see below
Video interview: recorded answers to on-screen questions, usually a minute or two each
Assessment centre or final interview: group exercise, technical interview, presentation, competency interview

Not every company uses every stage, especially smaller ones.
Online tests



































TestWhat it checksHow to prepareNumerical reasoningReading tables and charts, percentages, ratiosPractise timed; most tests allow a calculatorVerbal reasoningTrue / false / cannot say from a passageAnswer only from the text, not what you knowLogical / diagrammaticPatterns in shapesPractice sets; they get faster with familiaritySituational judgementChoosing the best action in workplace scenariosRead the company’s values firstGame-basedAttention, risk-taking, memoryCan’t really be revised; just be rested
Free practice tests are available from many test providers and careers services.
Answering competency questions: STAR
“Tell me about a time when you…” questions want a real story:

























SituationBrief context: where, whenTaskWhat you had to doActionWhat you did (say “I”, not “we”), and whyResultWhat happened, with numbers if possible, and what you learned
Prepare 6–8 stories that you can bend to fit common themes: teamwork, leadership, a problem you solved, a mistake, a deadline, persuading someone, something technical you’re proud of. University labs, group projects, part-time jobs, societies and personal builds all count.
Technical interviews
For engineering roles, expect to be asked to explain something from your course or your own projects. Be ready to talk through one project in depth: what it does, why you designed it that way, what went wrong, and what you’d change. Diagrams on a whiteboard or paper help.
Assessment centres

Group exercise: they’re watching how you work with others, not just whether you “win”. Bring quieter people in, keep time, summarise.
Presentation: short and structured. Answer the question asked.
Questions for them: have two genuine ones ready.

Check yourself


                  
                  1. Turn "we built a robot for a module" into a STAR answer outline. 
                  
                

S: first-year group project to build a line-following robot · T: I was responsible for the motor control · A: I chose the motor driver, wrote the PWM code and tested it against the speed requirement, and changed the gearing when it was too slow · R: it hit the target speed and we came third out of twelve; I learned to test early.

careers-and-development/cpd-log-template.content:
A blank log to copy into your own notes. Record things when they happen: by the time you apply for a placement or professional registration, you won’t remember the details. See CPD and reflective practice for how to reflect well.
The log

Example row: 30 Oct · Lab: characterising MOSFET switches · Practical · 2 · Measured switching losses and saw how they rise with frequency · A, B · Lab data and photos
Goals for this term

































Goal (SMART)Why (which gap)StepsDeadlineDone?
Reflection prompt (Gibbs, short version)
For anything significant, add a few lines:

What happened?
How did it go, and why?
What did I learn?

Review
Every few weeks: which goals moved forward, what’s stalled, and what’s the next goal?

careers-and-development/engineering-cv-o.title: Engineering CV outline
careers-and-development/engineering-cv-o.content:
The rules

One page is ideal in first year; two at most. UK CVs don’t need a photo, age or full address.
Tailor it for each application: move the most relevant things to the top.
Every bullet should show what you did and the result, starting with a verb: designed, built, reduced, led, tested.
Save and send it as a PDF named sensibly (e.g. Firstname-Lastname-CV.pdf).

Layout
NAME
Email · phone · LinkedIn · portfolio or GitHub link · city

EDUCATION
University of Warwick (WMG) · BEng Robotics Engineering with AI · 2026–2029
  Relevant modules: electrical power and motors, mechanisms and machines, ...
School or college · A levels / equivalent with grades · years

PROJECTS
Project name · tools used · date
  • What it does, your role, and one measurable result
  • A technical challenge and how you solved it

EXPERIENCE
Job title · organisation · dates
  • Responsibility + result, e.g. "Trained 4 new starters and rewrote the
    opening checklist, cutting set-up time by 15 minutes"

LEADERSHIP AND ACTIVITIES
Society roles, course rep, volunteering, competitions

SKILLS
Technical: MATLAB, Python, CAD, soldering, test equipment ...
Other: languages, driving licence, first aid

What counts for a first-year

Personal projects are gold: 3D printer builds and modifications, robots, coding projects, anything with a photo or a GitHub link.
Course projects and labs: what you built and measured, not just the module name.
Part-time jobs: any job shows reliability. Pull out anything involving responsibility, customers, problem solving or systems.
Society roles: committee positions (treasurer, secretary, captain) show responsibility and organisation.

Bullet makeover





















WeakStrongResponsible for the club’s moneyManaged a £X annual budget as society treasurer, processing N reimbursements and keeping accounts audit-readyDid a robotics labBuilt and tested a 3-mesh DC circuit, verifying hand calculations to within 1% using measured dataHelped with a projectWrote the PWM motor-control code for a group robot, meeting the speed target after two test iterations
Check yourself


                  
                  1. What's missing from: "Worked in a team to make a robot"? 
                  
                

Your specific role, what you actually did, the tools, and a result. Start with a verb and add a number if you can.

careers-and-development/finding-opportun.title: Finding opportunities
careers-and-development/finding-opportun.content:
Trackr
Trackr is a jobs platform for students that lists spring weeks, internships and graduate roles, with separate trackers by sector, including UK engineering and UK tech. Each tracker lists open roles in one place so you can see what’s open and plan around deadlines. It also has a CV template, CV reviews, guides and community group chats. There’s a free account and a paid Premium tier.
How to use it well:

Make an account and open the UK Engineering and UK Tech trackers. Robotics roles turn up in both.
Go through it once a week, early in the season (September–December), and note opening dates.
Keep your own tracker of what you’ve applied for (company, role, date applied, stage, deadline, notes). A spreadsheet or an Obsidian table is fine.
Apply early. Rolling deadlines mean the advertised closing date is the latest, not the target.

Other places to look





































WhereGood forGradcrackerEngineering and technology placements, internships and graduate jobs in the UKThe university careers serviceLocal opportunities, CV and interview help, careers fairs, employer eventsProfessional institutions (IET, IMechE)Student membership, events, scholarships, and employers who sponsor studentsLinkedInFollowing companies, and seeing who’s been on which schemesCompany careers pagesThe final, official deadlines. Always check hereLecturers and lab staffSummer research projects and industry contactsSocieties and competitionsRobotics clubs and hackathons, where employers often sponsor and recruit
Scholarships worth knowing about
Some institutions and employers fund engineering students with money, mentoring and work experience. The IET and IMechE both run scholarship schemes. Check their sites each autumn.
Check yourself


                  
                  1. A role says "closes 31 January" but is rolling. When should you apply? 
                  
                

As soon as it opens. Rolling roles can fill and close long before the stated date.

careers-and-development/skills-self-asse.title: Skills self-assessment template
careers-and-development/skills-self-asse.content:
Copy this into your own notes and fill it in at the start of each term. Compare it with the last one to see how you’ve moved. The five areas are explained in UK-SPEC and professional registration.
Scale: 1 = no experience yet · 2 = aware, little practice · 3 = done it with support · 4 = can do it independently · 5 = could teach or lead it















































AreaScore (1–5)Evidence: what have I actually done?Gap: what’s missing?Next stepA · Knowledge and understandingB · Design, development and problem solvingC · Responsibility, management and leadershipD · Communication and interpersonal skillsE · Professional commitment
Tips

Score from evidence, not feeling. If you can’t name something you did, it’s probably a 1 or 2.
Pick one strength and one or two gaps to focus on, and turn each gap into a SMART goal in the CPD log template.
Keep old versions. Seeing a 2 become a 4 over a year is useful evidence in itself.

careers-and-development/types-of-opportu.title: Types of opportunity
careers-and-development/types-of-opportu.content:
The idea
Most engineering employers recruit students through a few standard schemes. Knowing which ones are open to you this year matters, because the shorter ones are aimed at first-years, and many close months before they start.















































TypeLengthUsually forWhen you applyInsight day / open day1 dayAny yearThrough the year, often autumn and springSpring week1–5 days, around EasterFirst-years (some second-years)Autumn to early winter of first yearSummer internship8–12 weeks, paidMostly penultimate-year students, some earlierAutumn to winter before the summerPlacement year (year in industry)9–15 months, paidSecond-years, taken between years 2 and 3Autumn to winter of second yearGraduate scheme1–3 yearsFinal-years and graduatesAutumn of final yearDegree apprenticeship3–5 years, paid, degree includedUsually school leavers; some graduate-level schemesVaries; many in autumn and spring
Dates differ by company, and many applications are rolling: they close early once enough people have applied. Apply as soon as something opens.
Spring weeks and insight days
Short programmes to show you what a company does. They’re designed for people with no experience, so first year is exactly the right time. Some lead to a fast-track or guaranteed interview for an internship or placement the next year.
Summer internships
Real project work over the summer. Engineering firms mostly target students a year or two from graduating, but smaller companies, start-ups and research labs often take first-years. University research internships (working with a lecturer over the summer) are another route.
Placement year
This degree offers an optional year in industry. You’d usually apply in the autumn of Year 2 and go between Years 2 and 3. A placement is often the strongest thing on a graduate CV, and many lead to a graduate job offer.
Degree apprenticeships
You work for an employer and study for a degree part-time, with fees paid by the employer and a salary. They’re mostly entered straight from school, so for current undergraduates they’re more relevant as:

something to know about if you’re thinking of changing route (talk to the university first: you’d usually start again from Year 1)
graduate-level and master’s apprenticeships that some employers offer after a degree.

Search the government’s Find an apprenticeship service and company careers pages.
Check yourself


                  
                  1. You're a first-year in October. What should you be applying for right now? 
                  
                

Spring weeks and insight days, plus any first-year internships or summer research projects you can find.

tools/matlab-basics.title: MATLAB basics
tools/matlab-basics.content:
Getting it
Students can usually use MATLAB through the university licence, either installed or in the browser (MATLAB Online). Check the IT services pages for the current way to sign in. MATLAB Onramp, MathWorks’ free two-hour course, is worth doing first.
The essentials
x = 5;                 % semicolon hides the output
v = [1, 2, 3];         % row vector (commas or spaces)
c = [1; 2; 3];         % column vector (semicolons)
A = [2, 1, -1; 1, 3, 2; 2, -1, 4];   % 3x3 matrix: commas split columns, semicolons split rows
A(2,3)                 % row 2, column 3 -> 2
A'                     % transpose
det(A)                 % determinant
inv(A)                 % inverse
Element-wise vs matrix operations: A*B is matrix multiplication; A.*B multiplies element by element. The same goes for .^ and ./. You need the dot when applying a formula to a whole vector of values, like t.^2.
Solving a circuit
The Mesh analysis worked example in three lines:
R = [10, -6, 0; -6, 17, -8; 0, -8, 10];
V = [24; 0; 12];        % must be a column
I = R \ V               % backslash solves R*I = V
Use \, not inv(R)*V. It’s faster and more accurate. A common error is writing V = [24, 0, 12] (a row), which gives a dimension error.
Plotting an RC transient
R = 47e3;  C = 100e-6;  V = 12;
tau = R*C;
t = linspace(0, 5*tau, 500);      % 500 points from 0 to 5 tau
u = V*(1 - exp(-t/tau));          % note: exp works element-wise
i = (V/R)*exp(-t/tau);
 
yyaxis left;  plot(t, u); ylabel('u_C (V)');
yyaxis right; plot(t, i*1e3); ylabel('i (mA)');
xlabel('t (s)'); title('RC charging'); grid on
Printing results neatly
fprintf('tau = %.2f s\n', tau);
fprintf('I1 = %.3f A, I2 = %.3f A, I3 = %.3f A\n', I);
Scripts and functions

A script (.m file) is a list of commands. Put clear; clc; at the top so old variables don’t interfere.
A function goes in its own file named after it:

function P = mosfet_loss(Rds, I, V, ton, toff, f)
    P = Rds*I^2 + (V*I/2)*(ton + toff)*f;
end
Call it with mosfet_loss(0.075, 10, 24, 57e-9, 74e-9, 13e3) and you get 7.70 W, matching MOSFET power loss.
Common errors

























MessageUsual causeDimensions of arrays being concatenated are not consistentRows of different lengths in a matrixIncorrect dimensions for matrix multiplicationUsed * where you needed .*Undefined function or variableTypo, or the script ran before the variable was setMatrix is singularDeterminant is zero: check your equations

tools/scientific-calculator.title: Scientific calculator
tools/scientific-calculator.content:
Which calculator?
The computer-based tests only allow non-programmable scientific calculators. The Casio ClassWiz range is the usual choice. Check your module’s rules, but the fx-991 models are the ones worth having, because they do matrices, simultaneous equations and complex numbers. The cheaper fx-83 and fx-85 don’t.
There are two generations, with different menus (exact key names can vary slightly between versions, so check against your own):

fx-991EX (older): press MENU, then a number or letter for each mode.
fx-991CW (newer): press HOME and pick an app with the arrow keys.

Determinants and matrix maths
Used in Matrices and Cramer’s rule and Mesh analysis.



































Stepfx-991EXfx-991CWOpenMENU → 4 (Matrix)HOME → MatrixDefine a matrixChoose MatA, set rows and columns, type the values (= after each)TOOLS → define MatA, set size, type the valuesBack to calculateACACDeterminantOPTN → Determinant → OPTN → MatA → ) → =CATALOG → Matrix → Matrix Calculation → Det → MatA → ) → EXEInverseMatA then x⁻¹MatA then x⁻¹
Simultaneous equations
The fastest way to solve a 3×3 mesh matrix (show working separately if the question asks for it).

























Stepfx-991EXfx-991CWOpenMENU → A (Equation/Func) → 1 (Simul Equation) → 3 unknownsHOME → Equation → Simul Equation → 3 unknownsEnterType each row’s coefficients, then the constantSameSolve= and step through x, y, zEXE and step through
Check: for the system in the Mesh analysis worked example, you should get 4.457, 3.429 and 3.943.
Complex numbers
Needed later for AC impedance (Z_L = j\omega L).

fx-991EX: MENU → 2 (Complex). The imaginary unit i is ENG. Convert to polar with OPTN → ▶r∠θ.
fx-991CW: HOME → Complex. Same idea through the TOOLS or OPTN menu.

Engineers write j for \sqrt{-1}; the calculator writes i. They’re the same.
Repeating a calculation with different values
For tables like RC charging at 0.1τ, 0.5τ, 1τ…: type the full expression once, press =, then use the left arrow to go back into it, change only the t value, and press = again. Or use the Table mode with f(x) set to your formula.
Solving any one equation (SOLVE)
Type the equation using the variable X (ALPHA then the X key), e.g. 5(1-e^(-X/0.47))=4, then SHIFT → SOLVE (fx-991EX) or the equivalent in the Calculate app’s TOOLS menu on the CW. It finds X numerically, which is handy when you can’t rearrange easily.
Habits that save marks

Check degrees or radians (shown at the top of the screen) before any trig. Kinematics usually needs radians.
Use the ×10ˣ key for engineering powers: 470×10^-6 for 470 µF.
Store intermediate answers (STO → A) instead of retyping rounded numbers.
Keep at least 4 significant figures until the final answer.

wm199/cpd-and-reflective-practice.title: CPD and reflective practice
wm199/cpd-and-reflective-practice.content:
The idea
Continuing professional development (CPD) is how engineers keep getting better after their degree, and registration expects you to record it. It’s a cycle: work out what you need → learn it however suits you → reflect on what you learned → set the next goal. The skill underneath it is reflection: looking back at an experience honestly enough to change what you do next time.
Where CPD comes from

















AcademicPracticalProfessionalVolunteeringLectures, coursework, software, reportsProjects, competitions, prototypes, internshipsTalks, industry visits, institution events, societiesMentoring, outreach, running a club
The UK-SPEC CPD code asks engineers to own their development, do a variety of activities, and record, reflect, evaluate and review. They should also support other people’s development.
Gibbs’ reflective cycle


































StageAskDescriptionWhat happened?FeelingsWhat did you, and others, feel?EvaluationWhat went well and badly?AnalysisWhy did it happen that way?ConclusionWhat did you learn? What do you need to develop?Action planWhat will you do next time, and what help do you need?
The analysis is where most reflections are weak. “The meeting went badly” is a description; “there was no agenda, nobody led, and I didn’t speak up when I could have” is analysis.
SMART goals





























AskSpecificWhat exactly, and what are the steps?MeasurableHow will I know I’ve done it?AttainableIs it realistic for me now?RelevantDoes it link to a real gap or next step?Time-boundBy when?
Broad: “contribute more confidently in meetings.”
SMART: “In each of the next two seminars, bring one prepared question or suggestion, ask a peer afterwards whether it was clear, and record one improvement.”
Evidencing development
A good CPD record links goal → activity and evidence → what I learned → review and next action. Evidence is anything dated and checkable: finished work, feedback, a certificate, a before-and-after comparison.
Check yourself


                  
                  1. Make this SMART: "get better at CAD". 
                  
                

One option: “Complete the Onshape fundamentals course and model three parts from the lab rig by the end of term, checking dimensions against the drawings.”

wm199/designing-for-safety.title: Designing for safety
wm199/designing-for-safety.content:
The idea
The cheapest, strongest safety is designed in at the start: our ability to influence safety is greatest at the concept stage and falls as a project goes on (Szymberski, 1997). Operators, maintainers and the public inherit our design choices. A hazard designed out can’t hurt anyone.
Why it’s a requirement, not an extra

The law: the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 (s.6) requires designers and manufacturers to make things safe so far as is reasonably practicable. Robots are machinery under the Supply of Machinery (Safety) Regulations 2008.
The profession: the Statement of Ethical Principles puts others’ safety first.
The standards: ISO 12100 (general machinery), ISO 10218 (industrial robots), ISO 13482 (personal care and service robots), ISO 13849 and IEC 61508 (safety control systems).

Write safety as testable requirements: “The robot shall stop within 1.0 m when a person is detected ahead at 1.5 m/s”, not “the robot shall stop quickly”. Avoid words like adequate, robust and sufficient.
ALARP: risk must be reduced as low as reasonably practicable: keep reducing it unless the cost is grossly disproportionate to the benefit. Some risks are intolerable whatever the benefit.
The hierarchy of controls

The top levels don’t rely on people behaving correctly, which is why they’re more effective. Usually you combine several.
Inherent safety: design it out first (Kletz):






























PrincipleMeaningDelivery robot exampleMinimiseUse less of the hazardous thingSmaller battery, lower speed and payloadSubstituteUse something less hazardousSafer cell chemistry, soft outer shellModerateUse it in a less hazardous formSpeed and force limits in crowdsSimplifyRemove complexity that invites errorOne obvious stop control, no hidden overrides
Reliability isn’t safety
A part can be perfectly reliable (it does what it was specified to do) and the system still be unsafe, because accidents come from interactions and bad requirements. Safety is a property of the whole system in its real environment (Leveson, 2012).
Designing for safe failure
Assume failure will happen, then make sure it fails safely:

Define the safe state first (stopped, brakes on, lights on)
Fail-safe by default: power loss leads to the safe state (brakes that apply when unpowered)
Redundancy: duplicate critical parts
Diversity: different technologies (lidar, camera, bumper), so one cause can’t defeat them all
Graceful degradation: slow down, then stop
Monitoring: self-tests, watchdog timers, heartbeats

Barriers: prefer passive (physical, works without power) over active (detects and acts) over procedural (relies on a person). Prevention beats mitigation, and the barrier closest to the hazard is best.
The Swiss cheese model (Reason)
Defences are layered like slices of cheese, and every slice has holes. Harm happens when the holes line up.

Active failures: at the sharp end, with an immediate effect (a slip, a failed sensor).
Latent conditions: decisions that lie dormant (time pressure, unreliable alarms, untested software updates).

Don’t just blame the last person to act: look for the latent conditions.
Two analysis tools
HAZOP (top-down, team workshop, IEC 61882): apply guide words (no, more, less, reverse, other than…) to parameters (speed, direction, power, data, time).























ParameterGuide wordDeviationSafeguardSpeedMOREFaster than the limitIndependent hardware speed limiterDetectionNOPerson not detectedSelf-test, backup sensors, stop on sensor loss
FMEA (bottom-up, by component, IEC 60812): for each part, the failure mode, effect, and scores for severity (S), occurrence (O) and detection (D), 1–10 each. RPN = S × O × D; fix the highest first, and any high severity regardless.
Safe systems of work
A written procedure for doing a task safely:

Identify the task and hazards, step by step
Assess the risk
Choose controls down the hierarchy, and define the safe state
Write it down: a method statement, and a permit to work for high-risk jobs
Train, equip and supervise
Monitor and review after incidents, near misses and changes

Lock-out/tag-out (LOTO): before anyone works inside a machine, isolate its energy sources, lock them off, tag them, and prove it’s dead.
Check yourself


                  
                  1. Is a warning sign a passive, active or procedural barrier? 
                  
                

Procedural: it relies on a person reading it and acting. The least reliable kind.




                  
                  2. Name one latent condition behind the Uber 2018 crash. 
                  
                

Emergency braking had been disabled in the design, leaving a distracted safety driver as the only barrier.

wm199/engineering-ethics-and-duty-of-car.title: Engineering ethics and duty of care
wm199/engineering-ethics-and-duty-of-car.content:
The idea
Engineering decisions affect people who never signed up for them: the pedestrian next to a delivery robot, the person whose face it records. Engineering ethics is about how engineers should behave in their professional role: weighing consequences, duties and fairness, and acting when something is wrong.
Three ways to think about it

























TheoryThe ideaWatch out forUtilitarianismThe right action produces the most good for the most peopleCan it justify harming a few for the many?Deontology (duty)Some actions are right or wrong in themselvesRules can clash with good outcomesPractical ethicsDecide within real constraints, asking who benefits, who could be harmed, and whose needs countIt’s judgement, not a formula
The Statement of Ethical Principles
The Engineering Council and Royal Academy of Engineering set out five principles:

Honesty and integrity
Responsibility to society (people’s safety and wellbeing come first)
Accuracy and rigour
Leadership and communication
Responsibility for the future (across the whole lifecycle)

Duty of care
The obligation to use reasonable care and skill to avoid foreseeable harm to anyone affected by your work. In practice:

work within your competence
if your advice is overruled, explain the dangers
report suspected danger or wrongdoing
e.g. IET Rule 14: take all reasonable care to limit any danger of death, injury or ill health

Professional codes (IET Rules of Conduct, IMechE Code of Conduct) set these standards and hold members to account.
Four tests for a dilemma

























LensQuestionConsequencesWho benefits, who’s harmed, and how badly?Duties and rulesWhat do the law and professional codes require?FairnessWho carries the burden, and did they get a say?CharacterWhat would a trustworthy engineer do?
A good answer names the duty, the evidence and the person you would tell.
Real dilemmas

























SituationTensionLesson from a real caseA manager wants a delivery robot’s speed raised to hit a targetClient target vs safety of people who never chose to share the pathUber self-driving test car, Arizona 2018: a pedestrian was killed and the investigation blamed safety cultureA robot’s cameras record faces, and the team wants to keep footage for trainingBetter robot vs privacy. Identifiable images are personal data under UK GDPRR (Bridges) v South Wales Police, 2020: facial recognition use ruled unlawfulA known 1-in-500 failure, with a fixed launch date and “we’ll patch it later”Loyalty and deadlines vs a known public hazardChallenger, 1986: engineers’ warnings about the O-rings were overruled. Whistleblowers are protected by the Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998
A decision guide (Davis)

Define the problem · 2. Check the facts (and what’s uncertain) · 3. Identify who’s affected and which principles apply · 4. Develop options · 5. Evaluate them (harm, fairness, can you defend it?) · 6. Choose and explain · 7. Review: how do you stop it happening again?

Check yourself


                  
                  1. A robot passed 30 tests on a quiet route, but crowded conditions are untested. The manager wants a trial next week. What would you do? 
                  
                

One defensible answer: proceed only with modifications: a quiet route and off-peak times, a supervisor, a low speed limit and an e-stop, while gathering evidence for crowded conditions. Name the principle (responsibility to society, accuracy and rigour) and tell the manager the limits of the evidence.

wm199/hazards-and-risk-assessment.title: Hazards and risk assessment
wm199/hazards-and-risk-assessment.content:
The idea
A robot combines moving parts, stored energy, software and people. Safety means designing the whole system so that foreseeable failures and interactions don’t cause unacceptable harm. The tools are a precise vocabulary (ISO 12100), a way to score risk, and a register to track it.
From hazard to harm































StepMeaningRobot cell exampleHazardA potential source of harmA robot arm that can move fastHazardous situationSomeone is exposed to itA technician enters the cell to clear a jamHazardous eventThe thing that causes harmThe arm moves unexpectedlyHarmInjury or damage to healthA crush injury
A hazard exists whether or not anyone is near it. Keep the four steps separate, because each one is a different place to put a control.
Risk
\text{Risk} = \text{likelihood} \times \text{severity}
ISO 12100 splits likelihood into three parts: exposure (how often and how long someone is near), probability of the event, and possibility of avoiding the harm. Reduce any of them and the risk falls.
Same hazard, different risk: a fast robot arm is severity 5 either way. With the operator outside a locked fence, likelihood 1 → risk 5 (low). With a technician teaching it inside the cell at full speed, likelihood 4 → risk 20 (very high). Controls change the risk, not the hazard.

Score impact on safety, operations and cost separately, and take the highest. Matrices give rankings, not measurements: 1 × 5 and 5 × 1 both score 5 but need very different responses. They support judgement; they don’t replace it.
Where hazards come from
ISO 12100 lists mechanical, electrical, thermal, noise, vibration, radiation, substances, ergonomic and environmental hazards. Robotics adds software and control (unexpected restarts, sensor false negatives) and human–robot interaction (shared spaces, bypassed interlocks, cyber attacks).
Look across the whole life: installation, teaching, operation, maintenance and disposal. Most accidents happen in the non-routine stages, when guards are open and people are inside. Also consider reasonably foreseeable misuse, like reaching past a guard to save time.
Finding risks
Write every risk as cause → event → consequence.

































TechniqueHow it worksChecklists, incident dataCompare with known hazards and past accidentsWhat-if / brainstorming”What if the light curtain fails?”HAZOPGuide words (no, more, less, reverse…) applied to each functionFMEA (bottom-up)Each component: failure mode → effect → causeFault tree (top-down)From the accident down to causes, through AND/OR gatesSTPAUnsafe control actions in a whole system
The process
Determine the limits → identify hazards → estimate risk → evaluate (acceptable?) → reduce → loop back and check for new hazards. It’s a cycle, kept alive in a risk register with an owner for each risk, reviewed after incidents, changes and near misses.
Register columns: ID · description · cause · likelihood · impact · score · action · control level · residual risk
Controls
Always start at the top of the hierarchy of controls, whatever the score (see Designing for safety). The score sets how urgently you act, not which controls you’re allowed to skip. Controls usually reduce likelihood; severity only drops if the design changes (e.g. limiting a cobot’s force).
When it went wrong





























CaseThe failureFord Flat Rock, 1979First recorded robot death: no warning or safeguardKawasaki, 1981Interlock bypassed during maintenance, robot still poweredTherac-25, 1985–87Hardware interlocks replaced by buggy softwareUber, Arizona, 2018Pedestrian not classified, emergency braking disabled, safety driver distractedOcado warehouse, 2021Robots collided, causing a battery fire
Check yourself


                  
                  1. "The hazard is the technician being crushed." What's wrong with that? 
                  
                

It merges all four steps. The hazard is the moving arm; the situation is the technician in the cell; the event is unexpected movement; the harm is the crush injury.




                  
                  2. A risk scores 3 × 3 = 9 (medium). Can you go straight to training as the control? 
                  
                

No. Start at the top of the hierarchy (can it be eliminated or engineered out?). The score sets urgency, not which controls to consider.

wm199/sustainability-and-lifecycle-think.title: Sustainability and lifecycle thinking
wm199/sustainability-and-lifecycle-think.content:
The idea

“Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.” (Brundtland report, 1987)

Every engineered thing sits between people and the environment, so every project either helps sustainability or doesn’t. Lifecycle thinking means looking past the factory to the whole life of a product: where its materials come from, what it costs to run, and what happens when it’s thrown away.
The triple bottom line
A sustainable solution balances all three pillars, not just one:

























PillarAlso calledCoversEnvironmentalPlanetResources, emissions, pollution, biodiversitySocialPeopleCommunities, wellbeing, fairness, safetyEconomicProfitViability, lifecycle cost, long-term value
The UN’s 17 Sustainable Development Goals (2015, target 2030) are the global version.
The Engineering Council’s six principles

Contribute to a sustainable society, present and future
Lead with professional and responsible judgement
Go beyond compliance: meeting the law isn’t enough
Use resources efficiently across the whole lifecycle
Seek multiple views, including affected communities
Manage risk to minimise harm and maximise benefit

Lifecycle thinking


























PillarToolWhat it measuresPlanetLCA, life cycle assessment (ISO 14040/44)Environmental impact, cradle to graveProfitLCC, life cycle costingEvery cost: purchase, running, repair, disposalPeopleS-LCA, social LCAImpacts on workers and communities
LCA + LCC + S-LCA together make an LCSA (life cycle sustainability assessment). Partial versions focus on one thing, like a carbon footprint (ISO 14067).
Key ideas

Systems thinking: fix root causes and avoid burden shifting (solving one problem by creating another somewhere else).
Circular economy: replace “make, use, dispose” with a loop of reuse, repair and recycling.
Industrial symbiosis: one plant’s waste becomes another’s resource (e.g. Kalundborg, Denmark, sharing steam, water and by-products).

Applied to a delivery robot





























StageQuestions to askRaw materialsWhere do the lithium cells and rare-earth motor magnets come from, and under what conditions?ManufactureEnergy used, prototyping wasteDistributionPackaging and transportUseElectricity, including the compute for its AI modelEnd of lifeBattery disposal, e-waste, what can be reused
Check yourself


                  
                  1. A robot's new motor is 5% more efficient but uses a rare-earth magnet with a damaging supply chain. Which tools would show the trade-off? 
                  
                

LCA (environmental impact of mining vs energy saved in use) and S-LCA (supply-chain working conditions), with LCC for the cost side.

wm199/system-architecture-and-lifecycle.title: System architecture and lifecycle
wm199/system-architecture-and-lifecycle.content:
The idea
When you move into a new house, which change would be the most expensive and disruptive: repainting a room, changing the door handles, or moving a load-bearing wall? The wall, because everything else depends on it. The paint and handles are design; the wall is architecture.
Architecture is the few structural choices that shape everything else and are hard to undo. Design works inside it.

























Architecture is used to…Design is used to…Discover and refine the requirementsDevelop the individual componentsSteer the system towards its purposeBuild and integrate themChoose between optionsWork within the architectureDecide what to make and what to buyTrack configuration changes
For a delivery robot: wheeled or legged, how it gets between floors, and having an independent safety layer are architecture. Which lidar model, or the wheel diameter, is design.

“The fundamental concepts or properties of a system in its environment embodied in its elements, relationships, and in the principles of its design and evolution.” (ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010)






















PartDelivery robot exampleElementsMobility, perception, navigation, planning, fleet serviceRelationships (what flows between them)Perception feeds navigation; navigation commands mobilityPrinciplesThe safety layer can always override the planner; sensors are swappable modules
The same parts in a different structure behave differently. A roundabout and a set of traffic lights use the same cars and drivers but produce different traffic. In robots, centralised and layered control fail in different ways.
Decide early, while it’s cheap

Most is decided when least is known: the architecture is chosen at the concept stage, before anything has been tested.
Late changes cost the most: a change after build touches hardware, software and the safety evidence.
So explore alternatives early, while comparing them only costs paper.

Views: one system, several pictures





























ViewForShowsExampleOperationalUsers and operatorsScenarios and task flowsA day in the life: dock → collect → deliver → dockLogicalCustomers and managersBoundary, functions, data flows, interfacesContext diagram, functional flow diagramPhysicalDesignersParts, connections, standardsBlock diagram of sensors, computer, motors and battery
Every view exists to communicate something to someone. Draw the views the conversation needs, not all of them.
Decomposition
Decomposition means breaking a system into parts that can be designed, built, bought and tested, with defined interfaces between them. A bicycle breaks into frame, wheels, drivetrain (pedals, crank, chain, gears, hub), brakes and steering.
Where do you stop? When each part can have an owner, a requirement and a test (Kossiakoff et al., 2020).
A good decomposition is (Maier and Rechtin, 2009):

Cohesive: each part has one clear job
Loosely coupled: few, simple interfaces between parts
Owned: a team or supplier can be responsible for it
Testable: each part can be checked on its own

A standard plug and socket is the model of a good interface: any appliance, any maker, any room.
Building blocks, by what each one handles:






























BlockDoesRobot exampleSignalSenses and communicates informationLidar, camera, radioDataInterprets, organises, manipulates informationComputer, navigation software, mapMaterialGives structure or transforms materialChassis, wheels, payload bayEnergySupplies energy and motionBattery, motors, charger
Functional, physical and allocated architecture

Functional architecture: verbs. What must the system do? (Sense surroundings, plan a route, drive…)
Physical architecture: nouns. What is it made of? (Lidar, computer, motors…)
Allocated architecture: which part performs which function.


Trace it: requirement → function → part. Then, when one changes, you can see what else is affected. A requirement like “the robot shall stop within 1 m of a detected person” traces to the safety monitor function, which traces to the sensors, the computer and the brakes.
Auditing an allocation shows where the risks are:

























PatternWhat it meansA function with no partA gap in capabilityA function on one part onlyA single point of failureA function on several partsPlanned redundancy, or accidental overlap?A part with no functionWhy is it there?
Example audit: “detect a step or stair edge” with no part allocated is a gap, and a safety one. “Detect obstacles” allocated to both lidar and a bumper is deliberate redundancy, which is good for safety. “Plan a route” on software alone is a single point of failure, so it needs a safe fallback.
Functions that need several parts working together are often the hardest to get right. “Return to the dock” needs sensing, localisation, planning, driving and battery monitoring all at once.
The system lifecycle

“The stepwise evolution of a new system from concept through development and on to production, operation, and ultimate disposal.” (Kossiakoff et al., 2020)

There’s no single standard model (ISO 15288 uses six stages, the US DoD five phases), but they all split a system’s life into steps separated by decisions. Kossiakoff et al. use three stages and eight phases:

























StagePhasesWhat happens1. Concept developmentNeeds analysis → concept exploration → concept definitionEstablish the need, explore options, choose the architecture2. Engineering developmentAdvanced development → engineering design → integration and evaluationDefine the interfaces, design in detail, test the whole3. Post-developmentProduction → operations and supportBuild, deploy, use, maintain, upgrade, then retire
Each phase defines the next level down: system capabilities → subsystem requirements and architecture → component specifications → detailed design → parts made or bought. Even at the concept stage you have to picture the physical form roughly, or you can’t judge cost and feasibility.
Lifecycle thinking also means the whole life. For a washing machine that lasts ten years, most of its environmental impact comes from the use stage (energy and water every wash), not manufacture. Designing for the whole life (maintenance, upgrades, disposal) is part of the architecture too (see Sustainability and lifecycle thinking).
Check yourself


                  
                  1. Architecture or design? (a) choosing a 1.8° stepper over a 0.9° one (b) deciding the robot has an independent safety controller (c) choosing four wheels instead of tracks 
                  
                

(a) design · (b) architecture (a structural principle that’s hard to undo) · (c) architecture (it shapes the chassis, drive, control and where the robot can go)




                  
                  2. Write three functions of a delivery robot as verbs, and tag each as signal, data, energy or material. 
                  
                

For example: detect obstacles (signal) · plan a route (data) · carry the payload (material) · drive the wheels (energy).




                  
                  3. Why is an architectural mistake found during testing so expensive? 
                  
                

Fixing it means changing the structure everything else was built on: hardware, software, interfaces and the safety evidence all have to be redone, whereas at the concept stage it would only have meant changing a diagram.


Back to WM199, or see Systems thinking.

wm199/systems-thinking.title: Systems thinking
wm199/systems-thinking.content:
The idea
Widen a jammed three-lane motorway to four lanes and, a few years later, rush hour is about as bad as before. The new capacity changes behaviour: more people choose to drive, and the extra traffic fills the road. In US cities, traffic grew roughly in proportion to the road that was built (Duranton and Turner, 2011).
The lesson isn’t “never build roads”. It’s that a system pushes back, so you have to plan for how it will respond. Engineers meet this all the time:

Failures happen between the parts. The delivery robot works and the lift works, but the robot–lift interface doesn’t, and no single team owns that failure.
Optimising the parts doesn’t optimise the whole. The best lidar, planner and battery don’t guarantee the best delivery service.
Fixing one part can move the problem. A faster robot shortens deliveries but lengthens its stopping distance.

Systems thinking is one of the Royal Academy of Engineering’s six engineering habits of mind.

























Analytical thinkingSystems thinkingBreak the problem into parts; study and optimise eachLook at the whole, its purpose and its contextAssumes the whole is the sum of its partsFocuses on relationships, feedback and delaysExpects behaviour no single part has (emergence)Good for component design, calculation, testingGood for requirements, safety, architecture, decisions
You need both: analysis to understand the parts, systems thinking to understand what they do together.
The iceberg model
Only the top of a problem is visible. The deeper you go, the more lasting the fix:

Fixing an event (sending the robot again) helps once. Changing a structure (scheduling deliveries outside the lunchtime rush) or a mental model (what the service is for) stops it recurring.
What is a system?

“A combination of interacting elements organised to achieve one or more stated purposes.” (ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288)
“An interconnected set of elements coherently organised in a way that achieves something.” (Meadows, 2008)































PartMeaningDelivery robot serviceElementsThe partsRobots, fleet software, charging docks, lifts, staffInterconnectionsHow they affect each otherRequests, routes, lift calls, battery chargePurposeWhy it existsMoving equipment between labs safely and on timeBoundaryWhat’s in and what’s outWhich you choose depends on the question you’re asking
Is it a system? Check for elements, interactions and a purpose. A bicycle is (parts interact to give transport). A bag of marbles isn’t (elements, but no interconnections). A traffic jam is a system with emergent behaviour: the interactions are real, but nobody designed its purpose.
Changing a system. Swapping an element (a new sensor model) has the smallest effect. Changing the interconnections (how the safety layer can override the planner) has more. Changing the purpose (from delivery to inspection) changes everything.
Stocks and flows
A stock is anything that accumulates, and it can only change through its flows, at the rate they allow. A bath is the picture to keep in mind: the water level (stock) changes only through the tap (inflow) and the drain (outflow).

























StockInflowOutflowRobot battery chargeCharging at the dockDriving and sensingDelivery queueNew requestsCompleted deliveriesBank balanceIncomeSpending
This explains delays: even if you open the tap fully, the level takes time to rise.
Boundaries, subsystems and systems of systems
Where you draw the boundary matters. For the delivery robot you might draw it round the robot alone, the whole service (fleet software, docks, staff), the campus (lifts, doors, people, Wi-Fi), or the wider context (regulation, weather, university policy).

Too narrow, and the system surprises you: the robot passes every test but fails at the lift.
Too wide, and nothing can be designed or tested.
Nothing goes “away”: a discarded battery still exists somewhere, which is why lifecycle thinking matters (see Sustainability and lifecycle thinking).

Every system is a subsystem of something larger. Zoom in: a phone → its camera (subsystem) → the image sensor module (component) → the lens stack → a single lens (part). Zoom out: the phone → the mobile network → the digital economy.
A system of systems is one where nobody owns the whole. Maier’s (1998) five characteristics:

Operational independence: each part works on its own
Managerial independence: each part is owned and run separately
Geographic distribution: spread out, connected by information
Emergent behaviour: the whole does things no part does
Evolutionary development: parts change on their own schedules

Air travel is the classic example (airlines, airports, air traffic control, suppliers). You can design your own system but not the others, so you have to agree interfaces and assumptions with their owners. The delivery robot relies on the university’s lifts, doors and Wi-Fi in exactly this way.
How systems interact
Systems exchange four kinds of flow across their interfaces. A phone charger shows all four:

























FlowPhone chargerMaterialThe plug goes into the socketEnergyMains power into the batteryInformationPhone and charger agree the charging rateForceThe plug is pushed and held in place

























Interface elementWhat it doesExamplesConnectorEnables an interactionUSB-C cable, message bus, handover trayIsolatorPrevents onePhone case, rubber mount, firewallConverterChanges its formPlug adapter, charger, loudspeaker
Feedback loops
Draw arrows from cause to effect, marking + if both move the same way and − if they move opposite ways. Count the minus signs: odd means balancing, even means reinforcing.


Balancing (B) loops seek a goal and resist change. A thermostat is the standard example: it works to close the gap between the room temperature and the setting.
Reinforcing (R) loops amplify change, for better or worse. Late deliveries lead to more chasing requests, more robots in the corridors, more congestion, and more late deliveries.
Delays between an action and its effect can turn a balancing loop into an oscillating one, like an over-correcting shower temperature (Meadows, 2008).

Complicated vs complex





















ComplicatedComplexMany parts, but cause and effect can be worked outParts adapt and interact, so behaviour emerges and surprisesA watch, a jet engine, a gearboxRush-hour traffic, an ecosystem, a crowdAnalyse, specify, testAdd margins, monitor, experiment and learn
A robot is complicated inside, and becomes complex the moment it meets people. Perrow (1984) argued that tightly coupled, interactive systems will have accidents that design has to anticipate.
Why systems surprise us (Meadows, 2008)

Limits: the scarcest input sets the pace. More robots don’t help if the lift or the dock is the bottleneck.
Delays: effects arrive later than expected.
Bounded rationality: everyone sees only their part. Each person leaving a lecture at ten to the hour is acting sensibly; the corridor jam is nobody’s decision.

Leverage points: where to intervene
Meadows (2008) ranked places to intervene in a system. The higher ones are harder to change but far more powerful. For traffic congestion:

































Leverage pointExampleGoals and mindset (most powerful)Move people and goods, not carsRulesA congestion chargeInformation flowsLive journey times before people choose a routeLoops and delaysReal-time route adviceBuffers and structureSpare capacity on railNumbers (least powerful)Add a lane
Most debate happens at the bottom of the table, while most of the power sits at the top.
Why it matters

Requirements and safety come from the whole system, not just the robot: many hazards sit at interfaces (a robot meeting a person at a doorway) or come from behaviour (people reaching into machines), as in Hazards and risk assessment.
Architecture starts with the boundary, the subsystems and the interfaces between them: see System architecture and lifecycle.

Check yourself


                  
                  1. Is a pile of bicycle parts on a bench a system? What about the assembled bicycle? 
                  
                

The pile isn’t: it has elements but no interconnections or purpose. The assembled bicycle is: its parts interact to provide transport.




                  
                  2. Classify the loop: low battery → robot returns to dock → charge rises → (less need to) return. 
                  
                

Battery charge → need to return is −, return → charge is +. One minus sign, so it’s balancing: it keeps the charge in a working range.




                  
                  3. Adding three more delivery robots made deliveries slower. Give a systems explanation. 
                  
                

The bottleneck was elsewhere (one lift, or one dock), so more robots just meant more queuing and congestion: a limit, possibly with a reinforcing congestion loop. The fix is at a higher leverage point, such as scheduling or rules about lift use.


Next: System architecture and lifecycle.

wm199/uk-spec-and-professional-registrat.title: UK-SPEC and professional registration
wm199/uk-spec-and-professional-registrat.content:
The idea
In the UK, “engineer” isn’t a protected title, but Chartered Engineer is. The Engineering Council sets the standard for professional registration in a document called UK-SPEC, and licenses professional institutions (like the IET and IMechE) to assess people against it. Registration is independent proof that you’re competent, which matters most where the public’s safety depends on your work, as it does with robots.
The three titles

























TitleTypical routeFocusEngTech (Engineering Technician)Apprenticeship or work experienceApplying proven techniquesIEng (Incorporated Engineer)BEng plus experienceManaging and applying existing technologyCEng (Chartered Engineer)BEng plus further learning (or an MEng), plus experienceDeveloping new technology, leading, innovating
All three are assessed against the same five areas, at different depths.
The five competence areas





























AreaIn shortA · Knowledge and understandingThe science, maths and engineering behind your field, appliedB · Design, development and problem solvingTurning knowledge into designs that solve real problemsC · Responsibility, management and leadershipPlanning, managing resources, leading or contributing in a teamD · Communication and interpersonal skillsExplaining technical ideas to technical and non-technical peopleE · Professional commitmentA code of conduct, safety, sustainability and lifelong learning
Why it matters in robotics

Safety-critical systems: robots share spaces with people.
Accountability: who’s responsible when an AI system makes a decision? Bias, transparency and duty of care all apply.
Public trust: registration shows independently checked competence.

Degrees: AHEP
UK-SPEC covers people. Its partner standard, AHEP, covers degrees: the 18 learning outcomes an accredited degree has to teach. Every module on this course is tagged against it. See accreditation, AHEP and the IET.
Engineering identity
How you see yourself as an engineer, shaped by your education, your experience and your values. It isn’t fixed: a degree is where you start building it. A useful exercise is rating yourself 1–5 against each area with evidence for each score, then picking the gaps to work on (see CPD and reflective practice).
Check yourself


                  
                  1. Which competence area does "explaining a design trade-off to a client" fall under? 
                  
                

D, communication and interpersonal skills.




                  
                  2. Who sets UK-SPEC, and who assesses you against it? 
                  
                

The Engineering Council sets it; licensed institutions such as the IET assess you.

wm199/wm199-practice-questions.title: WM199 practice questions
wm199/wm199-practice-questions.content:
Short-answer questions on the professional topics. Answer in a few sentences, then compare with the model answer. There’s usually more than one good answer.
1. Split this into hazard, hazardous situation, hazardous event and harm: “A cleaner was hit by a delivery robot that reversed out of a lift.”


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

Hazard: a moving robot (its mass and motion) · Situation: the cleaner standing behind it at the lift · Event: the robot reverses without detecting them · Harm: impact injury.


2. A risk scores likelihood 2 × severity 5 = 10. What band is it in, and what should happen?


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

High (10–16): act urgently. Start at the top of the hierarchy, e.g. engineer out the reversing hazard (rear sensing, crawl-speed reversing), before relying on signs or training.


3. Rewrite as a SMART goal: “I want to get better at presenting.”


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

“Give a five-minute talk at each of the next three society meetings this term, ask two people for one piece of feedback each time, and record one change I make for the next talk.”


4. Which UK-SPEC area does each of these provide evidence for? (a) leading a lab group (b) a CPD log (c) explaining a design to a client


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

(a) C, responsibility, management and leadership · (b) E, professional commitment · (c) D, communication


5. A manager tells you to ship a robot with a known 1-in-500 failure that could injure someone, and to “patch it later”. What do you do, and which principle applies?


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

Raise it in writing with the evidence and the risk in numbers (at 300 uses a day, about one failure every two days), recommend not shipping until it’s fixed or controlled, and escalate if overruled. Principles: responsibility to society, honesty and integrity. Whistleblowing is protected by the Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998.


6. Give one environmental, one social and one economic question you’d ask about a robot’s battery.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

Environmental: can the cells be recycled at end of life? · Social: were the materials mined under safe, fair conditions? · Economic: what’s the lifecycle cost, including replacement packs?


7. Is “the robot shall stop quickly when it detects a person” a good safety requirement? Rewrite it.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

No, “quickly” isn’t testable. Better: “The robot shall come to a complete stop within 1.0 m of detecting a person in its path at its maximum speed of 1.5 m/s.”


8. Why is a light curtain better than a warning sign?


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

A light curtain is an active engineering control that stops the machine without anyone having to notice or obey anything. A sign is procedural and depends on people behaving correctly, so it’s the least reliable kind of barrier.


Week 4: systems
9. A delivery robot is late every lunchtime. Give an example at each level of the iceberg model.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

Event: today’s delivery was late · pattern: late every lunchtime · structure: one lift shared with the lunchtime crowd, and requests bunching at 12:00 · mental model: “deliveries should happen whenever someone asks”. The structure and mental model are where a lasting fix lies.


10. Is this loop balancing or reinforcing? Queue of requests → robots dispatched → queue shrinks.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

Queue → dispatched is +, dispatched → queue is −. One minus sign, so it’s balancing: the fleet works to keep the queue short.


11. Architecture or design? (a) an independent safety controller that can always stop the robot (b) the choice of lidar supplier (c) whether the robot uses lifts or stays on one floor


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

(a) architecture · (b) design · (c) architecture


12. In an allocation audit, “detect a stair edge” has no part allocated to it. Why does that matter, and what would you do?


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

It’s a capability gap, and a safety-critical one: the robot could drive off a step. Allocate it to a part (downward-facing cliff sensors), ideally with redundancy (two different sensing methods), and trace it back to a testable safety requirement.

wm199/writing-a-problem-statement.title: Writing a problem statement
wm199/writing-a-problem-statement.content:
The idea
Engineers are tempted to jump straight to a solution. A good problem statement stops that: it describes who has the problem, what it is, why it matters, and the constraints, without saying anything about the answer. If your statement mentions sensors or a robot, it’s describing a solution, and you’ve closed off other options too early.
Interrogating a brief
Take a vague brief like “The university wants a robot to move equipment between labs.” Before designing anything, ask:

































QuestionWhy it mattersWho sends, receives, uses, shares the space, pays, and fixes it?Defines the users, and who could be harmedWhat is being moved: weight, size, fragile, hazardous?Sets the capability and safety needsWhen: working hours or out of hours, scheduled or on demand?Capacity, and whether help is nearby when things go wrongWhere: doors, lifts, ramps, outdoor paths, security?Physical constraints and hazardsHow much to build, run and maintain?What’s realisticWhy bother? What happens now when things are lost or delayed?Proves the problem exists and sets a baseline
A good problem statement

Says who is affected, including people who aren’t users (pedestrians, wheelchair users, cleaners).
States the need and what success looks like.
Names the constraints: safety, budget, privacy, responsibility for faults.
Contains no solution.

Template: [Who] need a way to [do what], so that [outcome], without [harm] to [whom], within [constraints].

Lab staff need a reliable way to move equipment between campus labs at any time, so that items arrive safely, on time and traceably, without harm to people sharing the routes or to anyone’s privacy, within an affordable budget and with clear responsibility for faults.

Problem statements also hide ethical choices: “faster deliveries” says nothing about the wheelchair user on the same pavement. See Engineering ethics and duty of care.
Check yourself


                  
                  1. What's wrong with "Design a lidar-equipped robot to deliver parcels quickly"? 
                  
                

It names a solution (a robot, lidar) and only one measure of success (speed). It says nothing about who’s affected, safety or cost.
