wm1ad/week-4/electric-motors-and-dc-moto.title: Electric motors and DC motor types
wm1ad/week-4/electric-motors-and-dc-moto.content:
The idea
Weeks 1–3 got electrical power from the battery or the grid to the motor’s terminals. Week 4 is the motor itself: how it turns current into torque, the main types a robot might use, and where the energy is lost on the way.
The motors used in robotics









































MotorHow it worksStrengthsWeaknessesBrushed DCA commutator and brushes switch the coil current as the rotor turns. Speed set by voltage (PWM)Cheap, simple drive, easy speed control, good low-speed torque with a gearboxBrushes wear and spark (electrical noise); needs maintenanceStepperThe driver energises the stator phases in sequence; the rotor moves one fixed step per pulsePositions without a sensor; strong holding torqueCan miss steps; torque falls with speed; draws current even at restBrushless DC (BLDC)Magnets on the rotor; an inverter switches the stator coils in sequence (six-step)Efficient, long-lived, high power density and speedNeeds an inverter and position sensing; harder at low speedPMSMLike BLDC but with smooth sinusoidal currents (field-oriented control)Very smooth, precise torqueComplex controller, needs accurate position feedbackServoA system: motor + encoder + drive in a closed loopCorrects its own position, speed or torque errorsCost, tuning and set-up
Steppers get their own page: Stepper motors.
How a brushed DC motor makes torque

The stator (the stationary part) makes a magnetic field B, from permanent magnets or field windings.
The rotor or armature carries coils. A conductor of length L carrying current I across a field B feels a force F = BIL, at right angles to both the wire and the field. Force × radius = torque.
After half a turn, the same current would push the coil backwards. The commutator and brushes reverse the coil current every half-turn, so the torque always acts the same way. (A brushless motor does this switching electronically, with an inverter: see Motor drives.)

The generator effect happens at the same time. A conductor moving through a field has a voltage induced in it, e = BLv. In a motor this back-EMF opposes the supply, and it’s the key to how a DC motor regulates itself.
Worked example: a single loop
A single rectangular coil of active length 0.06 m and diameter 0.05 m spins at 2000 rpm in a 0.4 T field, carrying 3 A. Find the peak EMF and the torque.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

\omega = 2000 \times 2\pi/60 = 209.4 rad/s · r = 0.025 m → v = \omega r = 5.24 m/s
Each side: e = BLv = 0.4 \times 0.06 \times 5.24 = 0.126 V. Two sides in series: E_{max} = 0.251 V
After commutation the average is \tfrac{2}{\pi}E_{max} = 0.637 \times 0.251 = 0.160 V (the same factor as a rectified sine; see AC values)
Force per side: F = BIL = 0.4 \times 3 \times 0.06 = 0.072 N
Two sides at radius r: T = 2Fr = 2 \times 0.072 \times 0.025 = 0.0036 N·m
Real motors have many coils and commutator segments, so the torque and EMF are much larger and smoother.


The two equations that run everything
\boxed{V = I_aR_a + K_e\,\omega} \qquad \boxed{T = K_t\,I_a}

The electrical side: the supply voltage is shared between the drop across the winding resistance and the back-EMF, which grows with speed.
The mechanical side: torque is proportional to current.
In SI units, K_t = K_e (N·m/A = V·s/rad). See DC motor performance and selection.

What they mean in practice:

Speed is set by voltage. As the motor speeds up, the back-EMF rises until it nearly cancels the supply. That’s the no-load speed, \omega_0 \approx V/K_e. This is why PWM (average voltage) controls speed.
Torque is set by current, and the motor adjusts itself. Load it → it slows → back-EMF falls → more current flows (I_a = (V - K_e\omega)/R_a) → more torque. It settles where the motor’s torque matches the load.
Stall is dangerous. At \omega = 0 there’s no back-EMF, so I_{stall} = V/R_a, often many times the rated current. Drivers, MOSFETs, wiring and fuses must be sized for the stall current, or the driver must limit current.


Curves for a 24 V motor with R_a = 1.2 Ω and K_t = K_e = 0.06: no-load speed about 3800 rpm, stall current 20 A. Speed falls in a straight line as torque rises. Output power peaks at half the stall torque, but efficiency peaks much earlier, at light load. That’s why motors are chosen to run well below stall, not at peak power.
DC motor types: how the field is made




































TypeFieldBehaviourWatch outPermanent magnet (PMDC)MagnetsStraight-line speed–torque curve, compact, efficient (no field winding loss), simple PWM controlThe field can’t be adjusted; magnets can demagnetise with over-current or heatShunt-woundWinding in parallel with the armatureSpeed stays fairly steady as the load changesIf the field circuit fails, the motor overspeedsSeries-woundWinding in series, so it carries the armature currentVery high starting torque, roughly ∝ I². Used for traction and liftingSpeed varies hugely with load and it runs away with no loadCompoundBoth windingsA mix of starting torque and steady speedSome connections can be unstable
Why a series motor runs away: with no load, the current falls, so the field weakens. A weaker field needs more speed to make enough back-EMF to balance the supply, so the motor keeps speeding up. Lose the load on a winch or a robot and it can destroy itself.
PMDC is the robotics default: predictable speed (a fixed field), simple to drive with PWM and an H-bridge, efficient, and compact. Small mobile robots, AGVs and educational platforms nearly all use geared PMDC motors.
Construction

Iron-core: windings on a laminated iron core. Robust and cheap, from about 1 W to kW, 50–85% efficient. More inertia and some “cogging” (lumpy torque at low speed). Mobile robots and geared actuators.
Coreless (ironless): a self-supporting hollow winding. Very low inertia for fast, smooth response, 60–90% efficient, but expensive and limited by heat. Grippers, medical and precision robots.

Losses and temperature
Not all the input power becomes shaft power:
P_{loss} = I^2R_a + V_{brush}\,I + P_{iron+mech}
The three parts are copper loss in the windings, brush loss from the voltage drop at the brushes, and iron and mechanical loss (magnetising the core, bearing friction and air drag).
\eta = \frac{P_{out}}{P_{in}} = \frac{T\omega}{VI} \qquad \Delta T = P_{loss}\,R_\theta \qquad T_{motor} = T_{amb} + \Delta T
It’s the same thermal idea as a heatsink (see Thermal design and heatsinks), with the motor’s own thermal resistance R_\theta.

























T_{motor}Meaning40–80 °CNormal80–100 °CHot: check the manufacturer’s limits100–130 °CConcerning: check the insulation class> 130 °CBeyond typical insulation ratings
Efficiency isn’t one fixed number: it changes with load and speed (see the curves above).
Worked example: losses and temperature
A motor on 24 V draws 2 A and delivers 0.12 N·m at 3000 rpm. R_a = 1.5 Ω, the brush drop is 0.8 V, R_\theta = 6 °C/W and the room is at 25 °C. Find the efficiency, the losses and the motor temperature. What’s the stall current?


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

P_{in} = 24 \times 2 = 48 W · \omega = 3000 \times 2\pi/60 = 314.2 rad/s · P_{out} = 0.12 \times 314.2 = 37.7 W
\eta = 37.7/48 = 78.5\% · total loss = 48 - 37.7 = 10.3 W
Copper = 2^2 \times 1.5 = 6.0 W · brushes = 0.8 \times 2 = 1.6 W · iron and mechanical (the rest) = 2.7 W
\Delta T = 10.3 \times 6 = 61.8 °C → T_{motor} = 86.8 °C: hot, so check the rating
I_{stall} = 24/1.5 = 16 A, eight times the running current. At stall all 384 W (16^2 \times 1.5) becomes heat.


Common mistakes

Thinking torque rises with speed. It’s the other way round: more load means less speed and more current.
Sizing the driver for running current. Size it for stall, or limit the current.
Mixing up shunt and series faults. Shunt overspeeds if its field fails; series runs away if it loses its load.
Forgetting rpm → rad/s before P = T\omega.

Check yourself


                  
                  1. Why does a DC motor draw more current when it's loaded? 
                  
                

The load slows it, so the back-EMF (K_e\omega) falls. More of the supply voltage is left across R_a, so more current flows, which gives the extra torque (T = K_tI).




                  
                  2. Why is a PMDC motor preferred over a series motor for a mobile robot? 
                  
                

Its fixed field gives a predictable, straight-line speed–torque relationship that’s easy to control, and it won’t run away if the wheels lose contact or the load drops. A series motor’s huge starting torque isn’t worth that risk.




                  
                  3. A 12 V motor has R_a = 0.5 Ω. What's its stall current, and why does it matter?
                  
                

12/0.5 =  24 A. The driver, wiring and fuse must survive it, or the driver must limit current; otherwise a jammed wheel burns out the motor or the MOSFETs.


Next: using these equations to analyse and choose motors, in DC motor performance and selection.

wm1ad/week-4/sizing-a-drive-motor.title: Sizing a drive motor
wm1ad/week-4/sizing-a-drive-motor.content:
The idea
DC motor performance and selection and Stepper motors start from a motor and ask what it can do. This page runs the other way: start from the robot (its mass, wheels, speed, acceleration and the slopes it must climb) and work out the speed, torque and power the motor must provide. It’s the reverse problem, and it’s how you’d choose a motor for a new design.
The forces a drive must overcome


























ForceFormulaWhy it’s thereAccelerationF_a = maSpeeding the robot up (Friction and Newton’s second law)Rolling resistanceF_{rr} = C_{rr}\,mgTyres deforming on the floor; C_{rr} \approx 0.01–0.03 on hard floorsSlopeF_s = mg\sin\thetaThe component of weight pulling the robot back down
The worst case is all three at once: accelerating up the steepest slope:
F_{total} = F_a + F_{rr} + F_s
This assumes a hard floor, equal load sharing between the driven wheels and no air drag (which is tiny at walking speeds).
The method

Speeds: wheel speed n_w = \dfrac{v}{2\pi r} \times 60 (rpm), then motor speed n_m = G\,n_w.
Forces: F_{total} = ma + C_{rr}mg + mg\sin\theta.
Torque at the wheels: T_{wheels} = F_{total}\,r, shared between the driven wheels: T_w = T_{wheels}/N_w.
Back through the gearbox (it multiplies torque, but loses some): T_m = \dfrac{T_w}{G\,\eta_g}.
Add a safety factor (typically 1.5) for slopes, payload and wear: T_{m,rated} = SF \times T_m.
Power: P_m = T_{m,rated}\,\omega_m, with \omega_m = 2\pi n_m/60.

Then look for a motor whose continuous rated torque, speed and power all exceed these.
Worked example
A 30 kg delivery robot has 0.08 m radius wheels and must reach 1.2 m/s, accelerate at 0.6 m/s² and climb an 8° ramp. C_{rr} = 0.03, two driven wheels, a 10:1 gearbox at 85% efficiency, and a safety factor of 1.5. What does each motor need?


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

1. Speeds: n_w = \dfrac{1.2}{2\pi \times 0.08} \times 60 = 143 rpm → n_m = 10 \times 143 =  1432 rpm
2. Forces: F_a = 30 \times 0.6 = 18.0 N · F_{rr} = 0.03 \times 30 \times 9.81 = 8.8 N · F_s = 30 \times 9.81 \times \sin8° = 41.0 N
F_{total} = 67.8 N. The ramp is by far the biggest part.
3. Wheels: T_{wheels} = 67.8 \times 0.08 = 5.42 N·m → T_w = 2.71 N·m per wheel
4. Motor: T_m = 2.71/(10 \times 0.85) = 0.319 N·m
5. Rated: 1.5 \times 0.319 =  0.48 N·m
6. Power: \omega_m = 2\pi \times 1432/60 = 150 rad/s → P_m = 0.48 \times 150 =  72 W per motor
So you’d look for a motor of roughly 80–100 W continuous, about 0.5 N·m, at around 1500 rpm, with a 10:1 gearbox.


What changes the answer most





























ChangeEffectSteeper slopeF_s grows with \sin\theta; usually the biggest force by farHeavier robot or payloadEvery force scales with massFaster accelerationRaises F_a, but only during speed-upsHigher gear ratioLess motor torque needed, but more motor speedBigger wheelsMore torque needed for the same force, less speed needed
Common mistakes

Forgetting to share the torque between the driven wheels.
Multiplying by the gear efficiency instead of dividing. A lossy gearbox means the motor must supply more torque.
Degrees vs radians in \sin\theta on the calculator.
Skipping the safety factor, then choosing a motor that runs at 100% on the first ramp.

Check yourself


                  
                  1. Without the 8° ramp, what would the rated motor torque be in the example above? 
                  
                

F = 18 + 8.8 = 26.8 N → T_w = 26.8 \times 0.08/2 = 1.07 N·m → T_m = 1.07/8.5 = 0.126 N·m → rated 0.19 N·m. The ramp more than doubles the requirement.




                  
                  2. Why include a safety factor if you've already used the worst-case slope and acceleration? 
                  
                

To cover what the model ignores: heavier payloads, softer floors (higher C_{rr}), gearbox wear, temperature derating and battery voltage sag. It also keeps the motor’s utilisation comfortably below 100%.


Back to WM1AD, or practise in WM1AD practice questions.

wm1ad/week-4/stepper-motors.title: Stepper motors
wm1ad/week-4/stepper-motors.content:
The idea
A DC motor spins for as long as it’s powered; to know where it is, you need an encoder. A stepper moves in fixed, exact steps: one electrical pulse, one step. Count the pulses and you know the position, with no sensor at all (open-loop control). That’s why steppers drive 3D printers, CNC machines, pick-and-place heads and camera mounts: anywhere that position matters more than speed.
How it moves

The driver energises a pattern of stator coils, which makes a magnetic field.
The rotor (magnets or a toothed iron core) is pulled into line with it, to the position of minimum reluctance, where the magnetic path is easiest.
The next pattern moves the field on, and the rotor follows one step.

So:

Position = the number of pulses sent
Speed = the pulse frequency
Direction = the order of the pattern

The driver is essential. A stepper can’t run from a plain DC supply.
Types

























TypeRotorNotesPermanent magnet (PM)MagnetisedCoarse steps, cheapVariable reluctance (VR)Toothed soft iron, no magnetNo holding torque when unpoweredHybridToothed and magnetisedFine steps and good torque. The robotics standard: 1.8°, 200 steps per revolution
\text{Step angle} = \frac{360°}{\text{rotor teeth} \times \text{phases}} \qquad N_{steps} = \frac{360°}{\text{step angle}}






























Step angleSteps per rev0.9°400Fine robotics positioning1.8°200The common choice (NEMA 17 motors)3.6°1007.5° or 15°48 or 24Usable, but coarse
Microstepping
The driver can split each full step into M smaller ones by varying the two phase currents in small increments, following a sine and a cosine, instead of just switching them on and off.

N_{\mu steps} = N_{steps}\,M \qquad \theta_\mu = \frac{\text{step angle}}{M}






























Mode (1.8° motor)Angle per microstepPer revolutionFull step1.8°2001/20.9°4001/80.225°16001/160.1125°3200

Benefit: much smoother, quieter motion, with less vibration and resonance.
Catch: each microstep has less torque. Under load or friction, the rotor can lag behind or bunch up rather than land exactly on each tiny position. So finer microstepping is smoother, not necessarily more accurate.
The step angle is a mechanical property of the motor; microstepping is a control method in the driver.

Unipolar vs bipolar






























UnipolarBipolarWindingsCentre-tapped; only half of each coil works at a timeThe whole coil is usedDriveFour low-side switches; current never reverses (simple)One H-bridge per phase, so two for a two-phase motor (current both ways)TorqueLowerHigher: more copper carrying currentUseSimple, educationalRobots, CNC, 3D printers
Driver chips put both H-bridges on one chip and use current chopping: they sense each coil’s current and switch off the moment it reaches the rated value. See Motor drives.
Strengths and weaknesses

























StrengthsWeaknessesAccurate positioning with no sensorMissed steps: if the load exceeds the available torque it skips, and with no feedback it doesn’t knowHigh holding torque at standstillTorque falls as speed risesSimple digital control (step and direction pins)Resonance at some speeds: noise and vibrationRepeatable, brushless (no wear)Draws current even when holding still: heat and wasted energy
A 3D printer shows all of these. At power-on it has no idea where the axes are, so it drives each one into an endstop and calls that zero (homing). After that, position is just counted pulses. If the nozzle catches on the print, a motor misses steps, the printer carries on regardless, and every later layer is shifted. That’s a layer shift, the classic open-loop failure. Fixes are a torque margin, gentler acceleration, or an encoder (a “closed-loop stepper”).
The forward problem: is this motor suitable?
Given the motor (step angle, current and resistance per phase, inductance, holding torque T_h, microstepping M, gearbox G, load torque, motor speed S_m in rpm), calculate its performance and check it against the requirements:
f_{step} = \frac{N_{steps}\,S_m}{60} \qquad f_{\mu step} = f_{step}\,M \qquad n_{out} = \frac{S_m}{G} \qquad \theta_{out} = \frac{\theta_\mu}{G}
P_{phase} = RI^2\ (\times2 \text{ for both phases}) \qquad \tau_e = \frac{L}{R} \qquad T_{out} = T_hG \qquad SF = \frac{T_h}{T_{load}}
\omega_m = \frac{2\pi S_m}{60} \qquad P = T_h\,\omega_m \qquad \omega_{out} = \frac{2\pi\,n_{out}}{60}
Worked example
A 1.8° hybrid stepper: 2.5 A per phase, 0.9 Ω, 3 mH, T_h = 0.55 N·m, 1/16 microstepping, 5:1 gearbox, 0.4 N·m load, running at 150 rpm. The joint needs T_{out} \ge 2.5 N·m, \omega_{out} \ge 3 rad/s and P \ge 8 W. Is it suitable?


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

Resolution: 200 steps → 3200 microsteps per rev · \theta_\mu = 1.8/16 = 0.1125° · after the gearbox \theta_{out} = 0.0225°
Pulse rates: f_{step} = 200 \times 150/60 = 500 Hz · f_{\mu step} = 500 \times 16 = 8 kHz
Output: n_{out} = 150/5 = 30 rpm · T_{out} = 0.55 \times 5 =  2.75 N·m ✓
Margins: SF = 0.55/0.4 = 1.38
Electrical: P_{phase} = 0.9 \times 2.5^2 = 5.63 W (11.25 W with both phases on) · \tau_e = 3\text{ mH}/0.9 = 3.3 ms
Power: \omega_m = 2\pi \times 150/60 = 15.7 rad/s → P = 0.55 \times 15.7 =  8.64 W ✓
Speed: \omega_{out} = 2\pi \times 30/60 =  3.14 rad/s ✓
All three requirements pass, but with thin margins (the safety factor is only 1.38, and the power only 8% above the target).


Worked example: a belt conveyor
A 1.8° stepper drives a conveyor belt directly through a pulley of 10 mm radius, with 1/16 microstepping. The belt must run at 50 mm/s. Find the belt movement per microstep, the motor speed and the pulse frequency the microcontroller must produce.


                  
                  Answer 
                  
                

Belt per revolution = 2\pi \times 10 = 62.8 mm · microsteps per revolution = 3200
Per microstep: 62.8/3200 = 0.0196 mm (about 20 µm)
Motor speed: 50/62.8 = 0.796 rev/s = 47.7 rpm
Pulse rate: f_{step} = 200 \times 47.7/60 = 159 Hz → f_{\mu step} = 159 \times 16 =  2.55 kHz
Quick check: 50 \text{ mm/s} \div 0.0196 \text{ mm/pulse} = 2550 pulses/s ✓
In full-step mode (M = 1) it would be 159 Hz and 0.31 mm jumps: visibly jerky, and in the range where steppers tend to resonate.


Common mistakes

Treating microstepping as extra accuracy. It’s mainly smoothness.
Forgetting the gearbox in both directions: output speed ÷ G, output torque × G.
Using rpm in P = T\omega. Convert to rad/s.
Bipolar = one H-bridge. It’s one per phase: two for a two-phase motor.

Check yourself


                  
                  1. Why can a stepper position accurately without a sensor, and what's the risk? 
                  
                

Each pulse is a known, fixed angle, so counting pulses gives the position after homing to a reference. The risk is missed steps under overload: with no feedback, the error goes unnoticed and carries into every later position.




                  
                  2. A 0.9° motor with 1/8 microstepping turns a 5 mm-pitch lead screw. How far does the nut move per microstep? 
                  
                

400 × 8 = 3200 microsteps per revolution, so 5/3200 =  0.0016 mm (1.6 µm).




                  
                  3. Why do robots use bipolar rather than unipolar steppers? 
                  
                

Bipolar drives use the whole winding, giving more torque from the same size motor. The extra drive complexity (two H-bridges) costs almost nothing now that driver chips contain both.


Next: working out what torque a mobile robot actually needs, in Sizing a drive motor.

wm1ad/index.title: WM1AD · Electrical Power and Motors
wm1ad/index.content:
Block 1 · 15 credits. Electrical principles, power electronics and motors: how energy gets from a battery or the grid into a robot’s motors, and how to choose the parts that do it.
You’ll be able to: describe the main types of electric motor · calculate electrical quantities in actuator circuits · justify a motor choice from the application’s requirements · test motors against those requirements.
Assessment: A1 computer-based test, 30% (week 5) · A2 individual report built on the lab work, 70% (week 9).

Week 1: circuit fundamentals

Electrical quantities: charge, current, voltage, resistance, power, energy and efficiency
Kirchhoff’s laws: KCL, KVL, series and parallel, dividers and the power balance
Voltage node method: one equation for circuits with several sources
Wheatstone bridge and thermistors: measuring small changes in resistance
Power electronics overview: converter types, the components, and a MOSFET as a switch

Week 2: matrices, mesh analysis and transients

Matrices and Cramer’s rule: determinants and solving simultaneous equations
Mesh analysis: every current in a multi-loop circuit at once
RC transients: charging and discharging, and the time constant τ

Week 3: from the wall socket to the motor


AC values: peak, RMS and average


Bridge rectifiers: AC to DC, smoothing, ripple and heat


Power switches: relay, SSR, BJT, MOSFET and IGBT


PWM: controlling power by switching fast


MOSFET power loss: conduction and switching losses


Thermal design and heatsinks: thermal resistance and sizing a heatsink


DC-DC converters: buck and boost


Motor drives: H-bridges, inverters and stepper drivers


Week 3 interactive: the whole week on one page, with live models and calculators


Week 4: motors for robotics

Electric motors and DC motor types: how a DC motor makes torque, back-EMF, PMDC, shunt and series, losses and heat
DC motor performance and selection: the calculation chain, gearboxes, and checking a motor against a requirement
Stepper motors: steps, microstepping, unipolar vs bipolar, and the forward problem
Sizing a drive motor: from a robot’s mass, speed and slope to the torque and power its motor needs

Revision

WM1AD practice questions: test-style questions with hidden worked answers
WM1AD formula sheet: every formula from the module on one page

course.title: The course
course.content:
Overview
Robotics Engineering with Artificial Intelligence (BEng) at WMG, University of Warwick is a three-year degree that combines mechanical, electrical and software engineering with AI, aimed at designing and building robotic systems. 2026–27 is the first year it has run. WMG plans to seek IET accreditation for it (see accreditation and AHEP), and there’s an optional year in industry or research.
How Year 1 is structured
Year 1 is 120 credits, all core. You have to pass every module (pass mark 40%), but Year 1 marks don’t count towards your final degree classification. Years 2 and 3 count 30% and 70%.
Instead of running every module all year, the course is taught in blocks: three modules at a time, each with its own lectures, seminars and labs.





























BlockWhenModulesCredits1Oct – early DecWM1AD Electrical Power and Motors · WM1AC Mechanisms and Machines · WM199 Developing an Engineering Mindset15 each2Dec – early MarWM1AA Rapid Prototyping · WM1AE Programmable Electronics · WM1AF Engineering Systems Design15 each3Mar – MayWM1AB Mechatronics Sprint Project30
The first two blocks build the toolkit: circuits and motors, mechanics, professional skills, prototyping, microcontrollers and systems design. Block 3 puts it all together in a team project: design, build and test a robot for the end-of-year competition.
A typical block

Weeks 1–4: teaching. Each module usually has two lectures and a seminar a week, plus labs every other week.
Week 5: first assessment week, no teaching.
Weeks 6–7: more teaching and the last labs.
Week 9: second assessment week, for the reports.

How assessment works
Most modules have two assessments:























WeightUsuallyWhenA130%A timed computer-based test on campus (calculations plus short written answers), or a short individual portfolio or reportWeek 5 of the blockA270%A longer individual report, often built on the lab workWeek 9 of the block

You must pass every component, not just the module overall.
In the tests, a formula sheet is usually provided and only basic scientific calculators are allowed, so practise with the calculator you’ll use. Written working is often marked.
Group work in Blocks 2 and 3 is peer-assessed.
Each assessment brief says whether AI tools are allowed.

Study tips that have worked for me

Read the lab section of the brief before each lab, and photograph every reading. Your report depends on the data you take that day.
Finish every circuit calculation with a power balance and every kinematics answer with a units check.
Do the problem sets the week they’re set. The tests in week 5 cover everything from weeks 1–4.
